subsection: 1. The personal exercise and fitness area

notes.b: The personal exercise and fitness area is the part of the course where you take part in a fitness programme that you design yourself. It is practical: you perform the programme, not just describe it.
points: The area is active and purposeful participation in a personally designed exercise and fitness programme, which means you do the exercise with a clear aim rather than just moving around.
The programme reflects the performer's own interests and goals, so two students can follow quite different programmes and both be correct.
The programme applies the principles of training (the rules that make training effective, such as overload and progression) to the chosen methods and exercises.
notes.tip: Personal exercise is a context for questions on training methods, principles of training, FITT, warm-up and cool-down, and progression, so expect to link your own programme to these ideas.

notes.b: You do not do every type of training. You pick one method for the heart and lungs and one for the muscles, so every performance is built around exactly two activities.
points: The aerobic choice is one method: continuous training, interval training, fartlek training, aerobics or step aerobics, spinning, or indoor rowing. Aerobic training works the heart and lungs for a sustained period.
The second choice is one other conditioning and resistance activity (training that builds the muscles by working them against resistance): weight training, core stability or circuit training.
Only one of each is chosen, so each performance uses exactly two activities.

notes.b: The performance starts with a warm-up, which prepares the body for the harder work to come. The specification sets its length at five minutes and lists the elements it must contain.
points: The warm-up lasts five minutes and comes first in the performance.
It includes a pulse raiser, an activity that gradually raises heart rate, so blood flow to the muscles increases before hard work begins.
It includes mobility work and dynamic stretches, which move the joints and muscles through their range, so they are ready for the movements ahead.
It includes movements that rehearse the development section, so the actions to come are practised.
notes.tip: Warm-up is a regular exam context, so be ready to name its three elements: pulse raiser, mobility and dynamic stretches, and movements that rehearse the main work.

notes.b: After the warm-up comes the main part of the performance. It has two sections, one for the heart and lungs and one for the muscles, and together they last fifteen minutes.
points: The development section lasts fifteen minutes and is the main part of the performance.
The cardiovascular section (the part that works the heart and circulation) uses the chosen aerobic method.
The muscular strength and endurance section (working the muscles against resistance, to lift heavier loads or keep going for longer) uses the chosen conditioning and resistance activity.
The muscular strength and endurance section can be organised as a circuit, a series of exercises done one after another.

notes.b: The performance ends with a cool-down, which brings the body back towards rest. It lasts five minutes and has two parts in a set order.
points: The cool-down lasts five minutes and comes last in the performance.
Intensity is reduced gradually rather than stopping abruptly, so heart rate and breathing come down smoothly.
Static stretches then cover the muscles used in the performance, each held still, which helps the worked muscles to relax and lengthen.
notes.tip: When asked about the cool-down, give the order: first a gradual reduction in intensity, then static stretches of the muscles used.

notes.h: Setting the goal: performance or health-related fitness
notes.b: Every programme needs a purpose, because the goal decides which methods and exercises make sense. The aim can be one of two kinds.
points: The programme aims either to improve performance in a physical activity or to improve health-related fitness.
A performance goal targets the fitness and skills that a chosen physical activity demands, such as the fitness a particular sport requires.
A health-related goal targets fitness that supports good health, so it is about everyday wellbeing rather than success in one activity.

notes.b: A good programme is built in a logical order, so that each decision follows from the one before. Work through these steps in sequence.
points: 1. Set the goal.
2. Choose the methods.
3. Apply FITT (frequency, intensity, time and type) and the principles of training.
4. Choose the exercises.
5. Set the work and recovery periods.
6. Plan progression over weeks.
7. Record each session, so you can see what you did and whether you are improving.
notes.tip: Know the order of the steps and name FITT and the principles at step 3.

notes.b: A programme that never changes stops working, and an exercise that is too hard or too easy does not suit the performer. Progressions and adaptations solve these two problems.
points: A progression makes an exercise harder in small steps, by increasing the load, repetitions, sets, duration or complexity. Small steps keep the increase manageable.
Recovery can also be reduced to progress, by shortening the rest between sets or efforts, so the body has less time to recover.
An adaptation is an easier or harder version of an exercise, chosen so the programme suits the individual.
Press-up adaptations: on the knees or against a wall for an easier version, and with the feet raised for a harder version.
notes.tip: Exams use personal exercise as a context for progression, so give the ways to progress (load, repetitions, sets, duration, complexity, less recovery) and a concrete adaptation such as the press-up.

notes.b: Training only helps if you stay uninjured. Each safety rule below prevents a particular kind of harm, so learn the reason with the rule.
points: Technique and posture must be correct before the load is increased, because heavier weight with poor form is how injuries happen.
The load must be appropriate to the performer, so it challenges them without being more than their body can handle.
A spotter (a partner who stands by to help) is used for heavy lifts, so the lift can be stopped safely if the performer fails.
Equipment is checked before use, so faults are found before they cause an accident.
Fluids are taken to stay hydrated through the session.
The performer stops the exercise if there is pain or dizziness, because these are warning signs that continuing could cause harm.
The space must be adequate for the activity, so the performer can move without hitting people or objects.

notes.h: NCCA clarification: aerobic and anaerobic training
notes.b: The NCCA (the body that sets the curriculum) has clarified what kind of training the area can include. The training does not have to be aerobic only.
points: The NCCA clarification on curriculumonline.ie states that the training may be aerobic and/or anaerobic.
Aerobic training releases energy using oxygen; anaerobic training releases energy without oxygen.
A programme can therefore combine aerobic and anaerobic methods.

keyTerms.definition: Active and purposeful participation in a personally designed exercise and fitness programme that reflects the performer's interests, goals and the principles of training.
An activity that gradually raises heart rate at the start of a warm-up.
Stretching through controlled movement across the full range of a joint's motion.
Holding a stretched position still, without bouncing.
The fifteen-minute main part of the performance, made up of a cardiovascular section and a muscular strength and endurance section.
The five-minute end of a performance, in which intensity is reduced gradually and the muscles used are stretched statically.
A change that makes an exercise harder in small steps, such as more repetitions or sets, a larger load, longer duration, greater complexity or less recovery.
An easier or harder version of an exercise, chosen so that the programme suits the individual.
A partner who stands by during a heavy lift, ready to help if the lift fails.
An aim to improve the fitness and skills that a particular physical activity demands.
Fitness that supports good health, as opposed to the fitness and skill needed for one physical activity.

factCards.definition: A pulse raiser; mobility and dynamic stretches; movements that rehearse the development section.

factCards.term: Fifteen-minute development section: two sections in order
factCards.definition: A cardiovascular section, then a muscular strength and endurance section, which can be a circuit.

factCards.term: Five-minute cool-down: two steps in order
factCards.definition: A gradual reduction in intensity, then static stretches of the muscles used.

factCards.term: Designing a programme: seven steps in order
factCards.definition: Set the goal; choose the methods; apply FITT and the principles of training; choose exercises; set work and recovery; plan progression over weeks; record each session.
Correct technique and posture; appropriate loads; a spotter for heavy lifts; checked equipment; hydration; stopping for pain or dizziness; adequate space.

questions.prompt: Outline the structure of a personal exercise and fitness performance and describe the content of each part.
questions.model: The performance has three parts. The warm-up lasts five minutes and includes a pulse raiser, mobility and dynamic stretches, and movements that rehearse the development section. The development section lasts fifteen minutes and has two sections: a cardiovascular section that uses the chosen aerobic method, and a muscular strength and endurance section that uses the chosen conditioning and resistance activity, which can be organised as a circuit. The cool-down lasts five minutes: intensity is reduced gradually, then static stretches are held for the muscles used in the performance.

questions.prompt: Give two progressions and two adaptations for a press-up.
questions.model: Progressions: 1. Add repetitions over successive weeks, then add sets, making each change in small steps. 2. Reduce recovery, for example by shortening the rest between sets. Adaptations: 1. Press-up on the knees, an easier version for a performer who cannot yet manage the full exercise. 2. Press-up with the feet raised, a harder version.
